AFRICA OFFSHORE
DATE: 02 Dec 2025
COUNTRY: Gabon
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Struck by (not dropped object)
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Safe mechanical lifting
NARRATIVE:
While parking the starboard (STBD) crane following routine lifting operations, the crane boom was brought down
into the boom rest abruptly rather than in a controlled manner. This sudden placement generated an unexpected
impact load on the crane structure, producing a loud bang that was heard in the vicinity of the crane pedestal and
surrounding areas.
The abrupt motion and resulting impact load may have introduced a shock event into the crane’s hydraulic or
electrical systems. A process shutdown occurred minutes after this impact, and although the causal link has not yet
been fully established, the timing suggests the crane event may have contributed to or triggered the shutdown.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• Crane boom impacted boom rest heavily.
• Crane incorrectly lowered at the boom rest.
• Lack of experience of Crane Operator.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Mandatory contractor equipment specific training familiarization to be performed onboard and documented with
new crane operators.
2. Selection of candidates for temporary cover to be formalized with the minimum experience requirement for
contractor operations
3. New crane operators to be mobilized in advance to come offshore and undergo supervision monitored by the
facility crane operator for a defined supervision period.
4. Non-destructive testing to be performed at the crane's boom & cradle by 3rd party.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper lifting or loading
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate training/competence
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate supervision

FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Pressure release
ACTIVITY: Maintenance, inspection, testing
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Energy isolation
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
Contractor carrying out repairs on the Scale Inhibitor Injection system, the system was understood to have been
depressurised. As the contractor started to release an end cap, the cap was projected downwards under pressure.
The cap went directly downwards into a section of plant close to a walkway. This could have had potential to impact
personnel.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Failure to properly depressurise closed circuit.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
Learning 1. The process for managing valve movements during a leak test in response to a leak was not robust. The
leak testing procedure was not explicit about how to manage such a situation. Also no bridging document between
procedure and company Control of Work procedure.
Learning 2. Site team did not verify that the leak test system envelope was fully depressurised. Task fatigue and
normalisation of the risk were identified resulting in the Permit Authority deciding to de-prioritise some oversight of
the task.
Learning 3. The potential hazard created using 6Mo tubing and 316 stainless steel fittings at tubing geometries
outside of manufacturer recommendation was not understood. Knowing this may have influenced decisions around
controls such as exclusion zones and proving zero energy at the point of system being worked on.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Tools, Equipment, Materials and Products: Servicing of energized equipment/inadequate
energy isolation

DATE: 18 Nov 2025
COUNTRY: Namibia
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Dropped objects
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Safe mechanical lifting
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
Flex Joint strikes handrail creating 2 Dropped Objects. During the removal of the Flex Joint from the Riser Feeding
Machine (RFM) using the starboard crane, the aft sling of the Flex Joint became hung up on the RFM bucket. As the
lift continued, the sling suddenly released, causing the Flex Joint to swing unexpectedly.
The uncontrolled movement resulted in the Flex Joint striking and damaging the RFM track and the associated
emergency-stop device. The Flex Joint then continued its swing path until coming to rest against the starboard-side
handrail.
The impact dislodged two sections of the handrail, weighing 2.4 kg and 4.6 kg, corresponding to 377 Joules and 722
Joules of potential energy respectively. Both handrail sections fell approximately 16 metres to the Riser Deck below.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Uncontrolled movement - swing.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Accumulate incident information and ensure proper cause analysis and mitigating measures.
• Set expectations for supervisor 1 to 1 conversations According to: HSE Improvement plan.
• Computer-based training on lift planning.
• Onshore crane and lifting discipline lead and mechanical lifting focal point to discuss systemic standardized
management of lift plans on vessel.
• Onshore resources to audit the effectiveness of systematic approach to management of lift plan.
• Update procedures for laying out flex joint.
• Ensure OEM compliant cameras for starboard crane are installed.
• The material handling plan for the vessel will need to be MOC from original design - action.
• Inspection and testing required on damaged RFM structure.
CAUSAL FACTORS:

DATE: 17 Apr 2025
COUNTRY: Australia
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Dropped objects
ACTIVITY: Office, warehouse, accommodation, catering
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Safe mechanical lifting
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
During pallet racking activities in the warehouse, a forklift was in the process of lifting a pallet to the third shelf. The
load backrest of the forklift inadvertently contacted another pallet directly above (load approximately 240kg) stored
on the fourth shelf which dislodged and fell approximately 5.6m to grade. No personnel were injured. There was one
nearby person 7 meters away.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Incompatibility between the forklift (material handling equipment) in use and the racking system configuration
installed. The distance between shelf three and shelf four was 1350mm. The height of the forklift backrest was
1250mm. This left 100mm between the two and when manoeuvring the load into position resulted in the load above
being lifted inadvertently. The higher you lift the forklift mast, the more important adequate clearances become.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
Equipment Compatibility Must Be Verified - Ensure all material handling equipment and load types are assessed for
compatibility with racking systems before use or when managing change. This includes verifying dimensions and
manoeuvrability.
Critical Importance of Adequate Clearance - Maintain safe clearance margins between shelving levels, loads and
the material handling equipment, especially when operating at height.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)

of change

PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Energy isolation
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
IP1 observed visible bulging of a drain hose and proceeded to disconnect it. Although the associated compressor
had been isolated, the hose remained connected to the main drainage manifold, which was linked to 24
compressors.
The hose remained pressurized, and upon disconnection it struck the IP1 on the left hand and lower leg, and
subsequently impacting IP2’s hand as they attempted to assist. As a result, IP1 and IP2 were injured.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The task continued despite incomplete isolation: only the compressor was isolated while the hose remained
connected to a pressurized shared manifold, the hose’s visible bulging signalled residual pressure, and the plan
was informally changed without a full risk assessment.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
Recognize and respond to deviations, verify isolation across the entire system, and avoid informal adaptations -
promote a disciplined “Stop and Verify” culture that empowers pausing and reassessment when conditions change.

ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Safe mechanical lifting
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
Whilst lifting a pennant on deck as part of a lifting activity (~56.2m length, static weight 16.2 mT), a tagline was in
a basket arrangement around the rigging to provide stability. The tagline had a single wrap on the generator lifting
frame, used as an anchor point. During the lift, the involved person who had been on deck dogging the load in a safe
location, moved to a location positioned between the generator and stored deck boards.
As the generator tilted, it trapped the involved person against a stack of wooden deck boards. The involved person
received an injury that required Medevac to an onshore medical facility for further treatment.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The tagline became tight due to overlapping or wrapping of the tagline on the generator lifting structure so the
tagline bound up on itself, causing tension on the tagline anchor point resulting in tilting of generator toward the
involved person's location.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
Lift risk assessments to consider all elements of the lift moving or failing, including tagline movements or failures,
to help identify potential line of fire risks that could harm personnel.
Lift plans must identify and verify tagline anchor points rated for the planned loads that will be transferred through
the tagline.
The communication method(s) for the use of the Stop Work Authority for all personnel involved in the activity, must
be clearly understood and tested prior to activity commencement.

PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)

DATE: 30 Sep 2025
COUNTRY: Germany
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Dropped objects
ACTIVITY: Drilling, workover, well operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Bypassing safety controls
NARRATIVE:
When filling a mud tank with brine to prepare for cleaning of the tank, the transfer hose became dislodged, fell
towards the ground (2.6m) and began to whip. The hose struck the pump operator’s leg, who suffered a ruptured
Achilles tendon. The operator required surgery, classifying this as a Lost Work Day Case under IOGP guidelines. The
incident is considered high potential, as the heavy hose coupling could have caused a fatality if it struck the head of
the injured person when it fell.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The original configuration of the activity was changed by the work team to run the lay-flat ‘fire’ hose into the top of
the mud tank where there was no connection point. The pump was started without the hose being properly
restrained and flow was too strong for the arrangements, causing the hose to dislodge and fall towards the injured
person who was operating the pump at the base of the mud tank.
Before the change in the configuration of the work, the job had been considered low risk. The change in risk
introduced was not realised by the work team, who did not forecast potential movement of the hose.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
Immediate actions:
1. Immediately issue / communicate a site instruction (or similar) requiring securing of hoses and hose ends
2. As an instruction, or an additional step in the risk assessment for the main tank cleaning job, state a preference
to use a vacuum truck for filling, and if not available, acceptable alternative arrangements. Include hose type,
suitable pump sizes, hose securing to tank utilizing fixed points, protection against failure of the system (e.g. whip
checks) and position of people.
Preventative actions:
3. Committed to installing fixed hose connections to all tanks and chambers within the tanks to ensure hoses
remain fixed and secure during pumping activities.
4. Implement dynamic risk assessment programme: Personnel will need to be trained on this simple process
and when to conduct it (e.g. before each new task, a change, or a change in the mode of work or location). Such a
process will provide a ‘pause’ before work, giving an opportunity to review risks and team actions, even for work that
does not require a permit or formal risk assessment.

DATE: 08 Oct 2025
COUNTRY: Norway
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Caught in, under or between (excl. dropped objects)
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Safe mechanical lifting
NARRATIVE:
On 8 October 2025 on an offshore rig, a lifting operation was underway to land an 11.8 m, 2.67 ton bottom hole
assembly (BHA) into a storage basket on the riser deck. During the final positioning, the BHA made a sudden
uncontrolled movement. The forward end either contacted the basket edge, rotating the load toward the injured
person, or the crane made an unintended movement. The injured person was positioned in a narrow space between
riser guide posts with no escape route available. He had earlier climbed onto adjacent baskets and manually guided
the load several times to open covers in the inner basket. The BHA struck him in the chest and compressed him
against another basket. Emergency response was immediate, and medical evacuation was carried out via search
and rescue (SAR) helicopter. The investigation identified multiple human, organisational, technical, and task-related
contributors including lack of hands-free lifting, trainee crane operator without supervision, congested deck layout,
communication challenges, inadequate planning, and procedural non-compliance.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Hands-free lifting methods were not used despite being available, exposing personnel to the line of fire. The
crane was operated by a trainee without required mentor supervision, contrary to procedure. The lift was treated
as a routine task, and risk assessment did not account for congested deck layout, lack of escape routes, basket
orientation requirements, or blind zones for the crane operator. The BHA was landed the wrong way due to missing
communication, partly caused by language barriers. The deck was heavily congested, forcing the injured person
into restricted and hazardous positions to open basket covers and guide the BHA manually. No exclusion zone was
established. Several crew members were new in roles or on the rig, and norms for intervening or stopping unsafe
work were inconsistent. Organisational follow-up on competence, planning quality, and supervision responsibilities
was insufficient. These factors created multiple error traps and eliminated critical barriers.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
Lifting operations involving heavy BHA components require detailed planning that reflects actual deck conditions,
special equipment requirements, and correct use of hands-free practices. Exclusion zones and escape routes must
always be established and maintained. Trainee crane operators must only operate under direct mentor supervision
in accordance with formal competence requirements. Communication expectations with third-party vendors must
be clear, including language-barrier mitigation. Deck layout planning between logistics and lifting operations must

DATE: 21 Feb 2025

FUNCTION: Construction
CAUSE: Dropped objects
ACTIVITY: Construction, commissioning, decommissioning
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Working at height
NARRATIVE:
An operator was removing a grating panel with manual handling hooks on the weather deck.
During the operation, the grating unhooked from the manual handling tools and fell through the opening, hit a cable
gate before landing on the underlying deck, approximately 10 meters below. The grating measures 1x1 meter and
weighs 52,4 kg which gives a kinetic energy of 5149, 44 Joules. No one was injured, but under slightly changed
circumstances people could have been in the line of fire as the deck was not cordoned off and there was a work
team close to the area where it dropped.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The grating was not physically secured.
During job preparation, the work crew had not reviewed all the required safety measures before starting the job, nor
verified that they had been implemented, such as securing tools and equipment to prevent them from falling and
barricading the area below the work site. No supervisor present to correct.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• When working at height, it is essential to ensure that tools and equipment are secured to prevent falling objects,
in accordance with life-saving rules.
• When installing grating, it must always be secured with a fixed barrier, such as a shackle or wire/sling (the two-
barrier principle), as shown in the image to the right.
• Grating like this should be secured to the structure above the work area. The securing equipment should be as
short as practically possible.
• The area below must always be sufficiently cordoned off.

A worker was seriously injured when he fell from a height of 4.4 metres.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Two of the workers in the team were working at height. One worker was retrieving formwork beams from a stack
stored on the façade scaffolding surrounding the emergency generator building. The other worker was installing the
formwork beams on top of the shoring system towers. The worker on the tower was standing on loose and unstable
formwork beams. He was wearing a fall protection harness with a Y-line and safety hooks, which he had attached
to various anchoring points at foot height. When the worker loosened both safety hooks to move, he fell from the
formwork beam he was standing on. The fall protection method was unsuitable for reducing the consequences of a
fall.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:

• Ensure that contractors and subcontractors have a safety culture where everyone understand that they can stop
unsafe work.
• Ensures that main contractors and subcontractors carry out work at heights in accordance with internal and
external requirements and expectations.
• Competence requirements for using fall protection equipment must be made easily accessible to all roles.
• Follow-up and confirmation activities must be planned, executed and documented to ensure safe work at
heights.

EUROPE OFFSHORE
DATE: 05 Mar 2025
COUNTRY: Netherlands
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Caught in, under or between (excl. dropped objects)
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Safe mechanical lifting
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
A forklift driver’s ankle was struck by a spreader bar during offloading from a truck at the logistics base. There
were no lifting pockets welded onto the bar. In past lifting operations, the spreader bar had been placed on wooden
blocks on the truck bed and lifted directly on the forks of a forklift. This time the wooden blocks were not in place.
The truck driver and the forklift driver decided to lift the spreader bar off the truck by hooking hoisting slings
attached to the spreader bar and to the forklift forks, crossing them to reduce the length of the slings. During
hoisting, the spreader bar rotated and swung into the forklift cabin, hitting the driver’s ankle. The forklift cabin door
had been left open to improve communication between the drivers.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
1. Uncontrolled movement of the spreader bar due to hoisting the bar with slings hung from the forklift forks.
2. Forklift door left open for verbal communication.
3. Use of incorrect equipment to carry out the lift - it is forbidden to put slings directly onto the forks of a forklift, the
spreader bar was not equipped with forklift pockets, a forklift hoisting adaptor was not available, a crane lift should
have been utilised.
4. No lifting plan, job instructions or procedures in place, thus no management of change applied.
5. Inadequate induction and training for forklift drivers and visiting truck drivers.
6. Supervisor absent due to long-lasting illness, no official replacement.
7. High turnover of personnel at the logistics base.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Ensure all lifts performed with Forklift are covered by a procedure or lifting plan.
2. Specify the requirements for lifting operations in site training and induction programmes for the appropriate
supply base personnel.
3. Check that the equipment needed to adapt forklifts for the expected loads is in place at site, and Operators are
trained to safely use it.

EUROPE OFFSHORE
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate hazard identification or risk assessment
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate supervision
DATE: 01 Sep 2025
COUNTRY: Norway
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Falls from height
ACTIVITY: Construction, commissioning, decommissioning
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Working at height
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Work authorization
NARRATIVE:
On an offshore drilling rig, on 1 September 2025, personnel and marine crew were installing handrails on top of a
unit on the main deck. Handrail sections (60–90 kg) were lifted by deck crane to the top of the unit, where an operator
worked at height to receive and install them, using fall-arrest equipment. The operator initially attached his lanyard
to the stairs, then to handrail, and later to another section to reach the final corner section. To fit the last section, he
had to lift and adjust some of the handrail. The locking pins were weakly retained and the chain/carabiner secondary
securing arrangement did not prevent them from sliding out. The section of the handrail tilted and fell, pulling the
operator with it. He fell approximately 4.3 m to deck, landing partly on the fallen handrail. The incident resulted in an
LTI and a dropped object with calculated energy of 2733 J, with assessed potential for a single fatality.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The units were not designed to support safe work at height: the only structurally adequate anchoring points (lifting
eyes) were located below top deck level and were occupied by lifting bridles during installation, leaving no suitable
anchor points available. The operator therefore clipped his fall-arrest lanyard to a handrail section that was only
temporarily secured by a pin, chain, and carabiner. The handrail securing design was inherently weak; on the short
side of the container, the locking pin had only ~2 mm mechanical engagement and could easily slide out, and the
chain/carabiner arrangement offered a false sense of security. The installation and commissioning procedure
mentioned work at height and scaffolding, but did not clearly explain how the handrails should be installed or
secured, nor the purpose or requirement for scaffold. No scaffold was erected, and the crew changed the intended
installation sequence, requiring lifting and moving the section used as an anchor. Competence requirements for
work at height (Norog 113) were not formalised in the competence matrix; several involved personnel lacked formal
practical WAH training and were unaware of approved anchor point requirements. Project planning and follow-up
from onshore were insufficient, and the contractor equipment checklist process was not effectively applied.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
Work at height must never rely on temporary structures (such as partially installed handrails) as anchoring points.
Units that require routine or installation work at height must be designed with suitable, certified anchor points, or
work must be carried out from properly designed scaffolding or other engineered access solutions. Competence
requirements for working at height (incl. practical training and anchor-point assessment) must be explicitly built
into contractor competence matrices and verified before mobilisation. Installation and commissioning procedures
for vendor packages must clearly describe safe installation methods, including detailed handrail installation
sequences, locking mechanisms, and when scaffolding is mandatory. Work permits that bundle many high-
risk activities can obscure critical controls; large scopes should be broken into smaller work procedures where
necessary to ensure hazards and controls are fully understood. A robust equipment and project-follow-up process
is needed, including use of the correct contractor equipment checklist and clear assignment of onshore and
offshore responsibility for installation planning and oversight.

PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Safe mechanical lifting
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
In connection with a pigging operation on an offshore installation, several pigs weighing 35 - 40 kg were lowered
from a scaffold using rope, as the pig receiver was placed 5m above the turret deck. When the last pig was being
lowered, the knot loosened, and the pig fell onto the turret deck and then bounced outside the barrier and down
onto the tank deck. No one was injured and there was no significant material damage.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Upon retrieval of rope between pigs, the rope was jammed onto a handrail mounting and loosening the knot onto
the round sling. The rope and sling assembly had not been inspected after tugging it loose from its snag point and it
is believed to have loosened the knot. The need to lower the pigs from the 5m high scaffold where the pigging took
place was not included in planning and risk assessments. Issues of logistics and material handling were given too
little consideration, special lifting expertise has not been sufficiently involved.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Planning/risk assessment of operation - include logistic, not just the operation itself and ensure the right
competence is included
• Ensure that adequate area is properly cordoned off

CAUSE: Dropped objects
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Safe mechanical lifting
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
Collision between northern crane and derrick resulting in falling objects.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Three objects fell after the north crane collided with the derrick. The crane operator had been planning to perform
lubrication of the slewing ring with the logistics discipline responsible for some time, but this was changed to the
crane operator bringing along a deck operator who was being trained as a crane-operator. A helicopter was on its
way to the platform, and they had about 25 minutes to finish before the helicopter arrived. It was decided that the
crane operator was to perform the lubrication in the crane pedestal while the deck operator operated the crane.
The crane was lifted and swung out over the sea. The crane operator reminded to "elevate the crane-boom" to
avoid the derrick and then went down into the pedestal. The deck operator elevated the boom and swung the crane
towards the platform. After a brief stop to change the lubrication cartridge, the crane was topped up a little more
before it swung further towards the derrick. The deck operator believed the boom was topped up enough. The
walkway and the spotlight mounted on the right side of the boom were driven into the upper corner of the wind
wall high up in the derrick. At the same time, the crane was lifted somewhat and detached from the tower. The
crane shook, and the deck operator observed an object fall into an area where personnel were normally present.
After receiving information about what had happened over the radio, the crane operator came to the cabin, took
over, and lowered the crane into the cradle. The logistics discipline responsible heard what was being said on the
radio, responded, and found the spotlight in a pallet with wooden lids in the moonpool area. A section of weather
protection from the derrick was found a few minutes later, and a bracket for securing electrical cables was found
three days later on a walkway one level above the moonpool area.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Use of anti-collision systems on offshore cranes.
• Certified safety training for crane operators.
• A forum should be established where instructors and trainees can share experiences during the training process.
• The management on installations that have personnel undergoing crane operator training should be informed
and make this more visible within the organization.

PEOPLE (ACTS): Inattention/Lack of Awareness: Improper decision making or lack of judgment

DATE: 29 Aug 2025
COUNTRY: Norway
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Exposure noise, chemical, biological, vibration, extreme temperature
ACTIVITY: Maintenance, inspection, testing
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Bypassing safety controls
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Work authorization
NARRATIVE:
Two personnel experienced symptoms of severe oxygen deficiency during inspection work, but managed to self-
evacuate safely. Subsequent measurements confirmed low oxygen levels inside the enclosure, linked to nitrogen
ingress from the turbine seal system combined with a lack of ventilation.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The incident was triggered by nitrogen leakage from the seal system, which under normal ventilated conditions is
harmless. However, following a planned emergency shutdown (ESD) and blackstart prior to shutdown period, key
barriers were unavailable: ventilation remained off, and the fire dampers which require manual reopening, stayed
closed. Without airflow, oxygen was gradually displaced overnight creating a hazardous atmosphere that posed a
serious risk of unconsciousness and fatality.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
Assess feasibility of installing fixed oxygen monitoring in the turbine enclosure and similar areas. If not feasible,
require mandatory portable gas testing before entry into locations with potential oxygen depletion risk.
Review and update the blackstart procedure to ensure turbine hood ventilation and dampers are restored before the
area is reclassified as safe for entry.
Revise PTW requirements for entries into the turbine enclosure during or after special operational states (e.g.,
blackstart, shutdown, or loss of HVAC). The PTW must account for potential atmospheric changes, with mandatory
portable gas measurements under such conditions.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Protective Systems: Inadequate/defective guards or protective barriers
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Tools, Equipment, Materials and Products: Inadequate design/specification/management
of change
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Work Place Hazards: Hazardous atmosphere (explosive/toxic/asphyxiant)

Safety performance indicators – 2025 data: High potential event reports
EUROPE OFFSHORE
DATE: 02 Jul 2025
COUNTRY: Norway
FUNCTION: Construction
CAUSE: Dropped objects
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Working at height
NARRATIVE:
During preparations for installing a 20’’ sealing ring on the platform on 2 July 2025, a technician tested the ring
for fit before the lift operation. The 7.1 kg ring slipped from the technician’s hands and fell 6.35 meters to the deck
below, landing approximately two meters from a mechanic who was grinding at deck level. The ring then bounced
and struck the mechanic on the arm. The mechanic received a first-aid level impact with no observable injury. The
event had a severe potential for fatality due to the weight and fall height. The ring had been brought into the elevated
work area earlier than planned, the area was insufficiently barricaded, and the test occurred without notification to
the crew below. Multiple procedural, communication and barrier-management weaknesses contributed.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The sealing ring was tested earlier than planned, without expanding the barricaded area and without informing
the crew below. The ring slipped due to inadequate handling conditions (gloves, oily surface). The work area had
been split into two phases, but equipment was still placed in the elevated area during phase one, creating exposure
before barriers were in place. Barricading was too small, based on a common but unsafe practice of using minimal
exclusion zones for “non-loose object” work at height. Communication between team members and between teams
and was incomplete. The area technician approved only the intent of barricading but did not verify it physically. The
team lead was cognitively overloaded and new in the role, reducing situational awareness. Stop-work authority was
not used despite unease among personnel below. The net result was coexistence of workers above and below with
no effective barrier against dropped objects.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
All work at height must assume potential for falling objects and require full barricading unless a technical barrier
(e.g., safety net) is installed. Equipment must not be brought into elevated areas before controls are in place. Area
technicians must physically verify barricades before work starts. Practices that rely on personnel remembering
not to bring loose items into height work are insufficient; technical and organizational barriers must supplement
human behaviour. SIMOPS coordination must be strengthened, including explicit identification of all nearby work
teams and discussion in morning meetings. Communication internally within teams must be improved to ensure
shared situational awareness. Stop-work authority must be normalised, supported, and used proactively. Project-
wide learning should be shared across platforms to eliminate similar practices elsewhere.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Inattention/Lack of Awareness: Improper decision making or lack of judgment
PEOPLE (ACTS): Inattention/Lack of Awareness: Lack of attention/distracted by other concerns/stress

MIDDLE EAST ONSHORE
DATE: 09 Sep 2025
COUNTRY: Bahrain
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Dropped objects
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Safe mechanical lifting
NARRATIVE:
During the night shift, the crew attempted to release an anchor latch tool from a permanent packer using a straight
pull of 60 klbs (including 55 klbs string weight) without success. Following contractors’ procedures, the string
was tensioned with 5 klbs over string weight and rotated manually, but no movement was observed. Based on
contractors’ instructions, power tongs were partially used due to the absence of a power swivel on site.
During the sixth right-hand turn with a 5 klbs overpull, the 2-7/8" tubing coupling connected to the safety valve backed
off and fell approximately 21 ft onto the rig floor, then a further 14 ft to the ground. At the same time, the tubing string
settled approximately 6 ft into the packer. The combined weight of the coupling and safety valve was 36.5 kg.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
1. Uncontrolled rotation using a power tong led to the tubing connection backing off.
2. Thread make-up integrity was not sufficient for rotation under tension.
3. Lack of appropriate equipment (power swivel) resulted in the use of a higher-risk alternative.
4. Dropped-object controls were inadequate, allowing heavy equipment to fall from height.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Management of Change (MoC) must be applied before deviation.
Any deviation from approved procedures, tooling, or operating limits shall be formally reviewed, risk-assessed, and
approved through the MBPS MoC process prior to execution.
2. Operations must stop when normal operating parameters are exceeded.
When loads, methods, or equipment differ from the original plan, supervisors must stop work and reassess using
approved Operator procedures and MoC requirements.
3. Contractually required equipment must be available and used as intended.
Operations shall not proceed unless all contract-specified rig equipment is present, functional, and fit for purpose.
Temporary or partial substitutions are not acceptable.
4. Stop Work Authority (SWA) must be actively exercised and enforced.
All personnel are required to stop work when unsafe conditions exist, including dropped-object exposure, lack of
secondary retention, or use of non-approved tools or methods.
5. Secondary retention is mandatory for elevated components.
All elevated or moving tools and components shall be secured with secondary retention wherever practicable to
prevent dropped-object incidents.
6. Roles and scopes of work must be clearly understood and respected.

During space-out of the traveling block to function-test the power tong, the Driller hoisted the traveling block with
the working string. When the string was about 2 meters above the rig floor, the Driller applied the brake. At that
moment, the traveling block and working string suddenly moved down to the rig floor. Work string landed on the slip
and travelling block stopped moving where the brake was activated.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
1. Roustabout washed the draw-works with diesel and Jet cleaner without recognizing the hazards of contamination
of the Draw-work system which could cause loss of brake friction and inconsistent contact with brake Rim.
2. The Driller did not supervise RA on how to clean the draw work to avoid any contamination and decided to leave
him alone.
3. No SOP or work instruction available for cleaning the draw works / brake rim, leading to use of unauthorized
cleaning material.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Update and revise JSA, SOP for cleaning in critical hoist equipment.
2. Ensure Regular competency is conducted to crew to Enhance Awareness and alertness.
3. Always maintain safe distance for space-out and retain mitigated plan for unexpected event while testing and
restart after repair.
4. Ensure controlled load test, no load must be attached to hoisting system while testing the system

materials/products

COUNTRY: Qatar
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Pressure release
ACTIVITY: Maintenance, inspection, testing
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Energy isolation
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
A contractor mechanical field service representative and mechanical team had disconnected the export gas
compressor gas turbine’s primary and secondary flexible fuel gas hoses. After disconnecting the hoses, the
contractor field service representative was on the back side of the gas turbine while the mechanical technicians
were on the front side. While lying beneath the gas turbine to check the water wash drain tube under the gas
turbine, pressure was released, causing the loose hoses to swing.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
One of the loose hoses struck the helmet of the mechanical field service representative, resulting in physical
damage to the helmet.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Trapped pressure must always be safely discharged before disconnecting components, even when the system
appears isolated - especially in high-pressure gas systems.
• Contractor activities must be fully integrated into company isolation procedures, including proper
documentation in Process Isolation Certificates, to avoid oversight of critical steps.
• Safe Work Method Statements (SWMS) must include detailed, step-by-step instructions, particularly for non-
routine tasks, to ensure consistent understanding and execution.
• Non-routine activities require Task Risk Assessments (TRA) regardless of pressure levels or perceived risk, as
they often involve unexpected hazards.
• System manipulations (e.g., Programmable Logic Controller forcing) must not occur without coordination and
approval from the Area Authority, and only after confirming all personnel are in safe positions.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Tools, Equipment, Materials and Products: Servicing of energized equipment/inadequate
energy isolation
PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Protective Methods: Equipment or materials not secured
PEOPLE (ACTS): Inattention/Lack of Awareness: Improper decision making or lack of judgment
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate work standards/procedures

NARRATIVE:
A gate door (two sections) of the Blasting Shop toppled over due to strong winds (approximately 16m/s). Each door

stand, resulting in damage to the cladding and frame. The incident occurred next to a pedestrian walkway, but no

WHAT WENT WRONG:

design.
• The necessary actions were not taken to address the inspection findings, including damaged hinges and
inadequate lubrication.

• Follow approved design drawings and specifications to maintain integrity and ensure safety of gates.
• Ensure that a quality inspection for weld hinges is conducted on all gates.
• Ensure that regular inspection and maintenance, including lubrication, are conducted for all gates.
• The operational manual for gates shall be provided and included into the Job Safety Analysis (JSA).
• All gates to be operated within the design limits by trained personnel to prevent damage of gates/hinges.
• Ensure that gates to blasting and painting bays are open during heavy winds to allow for unobstructed airflow.
• During windy conditions, all movable objects/equipment/tools should be properly secured/stored

FUNCTION: Construction
CAUSE: Dropped objects
ACTIVITY: Transport - Land
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Bypassing safety controls
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
A trailer driver was transporting six concrete barriers (3.5t each) on a flatbed trailer. The barriers were stacked in
two rows (three in each row), with one cargo lashing belt securing two concrete barriers each. While the trailer was
travelling on the bumpy road, the driver noticed that one of the lashing belts securing the rear concrete barriers
had broken, causing the load to shift slightly towards the edge of the trailer. He pulled over to address the situation.
Fortunately, no injuries or damage occurred.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• The concrete barriers were loaded onto the truck without appropriate measures in place - no dunnage was used
and there was inadequate load restraint.
• The driver used improvised lashing belts without proper inspection. One of these improvised belts broke during
transportation on the bumpy road.
• The driver did not recognise the risk of using defective and improvised lashing belts.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Always ensure all loads are properly loaded and restrained in accordance with appropriate lashing protocols to
prevent them from shifting during transportation.
• Always use additional support systems like rubber mats and/or dunnage to increase the clamp down effect
(friction between the load and the trailer surface) to prevent the load from shifting.
• Always ensure loading crews and driver clearly understand the importance of the pre-trip Inspection – lashing
belts and tools must be thoroughly inspected for wear, damage, and suitability before departure. Early detection
of weakened or compromised equipment can prevent incidents.
• Always ensure corrective actions are implemented at the earliest opportunity to prevent recurrence of similar
incidents/accidents – there was a similar incident three months earlier.

FUNCTION: Construction

PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire

NARRATIVE:
A telehandler operator was moving a 714kg pipe spool when he observed a trailer blocking his access. The operator
pulled the telehandler over to the side waiting for the trailer to move away. When the trailer moved, the operator
started to reverse the telehandler. After reversing approximately 2 metres, the front right tyre of the telehandler
failed and exploded. The release of pressure ejected the tyre 7 metres away from the telehandler. The primary
locking rim (weight 19.3kg) and the secondary locking rim (weight 2.3kg) were ejected from the split rim, causing
the primary locking rim to land 50 metres away and the secondary locking rim to land 70 metres away. No injuries
were reported. The Flagman and Rigger were positioned behind the telehandler approximately 5 metres away.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• Incorrect installation and assembly of tyre/wheel rim.
• During manoeuvring, the load could have potentially shifted to the right side of the forks due to incorrect
securing of the pipe spool.
• Over-pressure within the tyre (pinch resulting in the failure of the tyre innertube).
• The daily telehandler checklist does not include tyre condition or tyre pressure. Three tyres were found to be
new, and one tyre was damaged.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Equipment operators should be provided with tyre pressure gauges to ensure adequate tyre pressure.
• Improvement of daily checklists with option of multiple languages and requirement of checking tyre pressures.
• On-the-Job Training (OJT) on tyre pressures/condition and the use of gauges to be provided to all equipment
operators.
• OJT training video to be prepared to demonstrate the correct installation method of tyre and rims. To be shown
to all Plant Maintenance & Vehicle (PMV) team members who are assigned the task of changing tyres.
• All subcontractors PMV groups to identify and physically check all vehicles and equipment on the project that
are fitted with split rim wheels. Any vehicle that is identified as having incorrectly fitted spilt rims or misaligned
parts should be taken out of service until rectified.

FUNCTION: Construction
CAUSE: Struck by (not dropped object)
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Safe mechanical lifting
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
An 800-ton crawler crane and a 280-ton crawler crane had concluded lifting operations and were idle. A civil crew
requested the 800-ton crane operator to reposition the hook so they could avoid working under it. While slewing, the
boom tip section of the 800-ton crawler crane contacted the wire rope of the stationary 280-ton crawler crane. The
crane was operating within a barricaded area. No visible damage was found on both crawler cranes, and there were
no injuries
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• The 800-ton crane operator slewed the crane without the presence of the rigging crew or Signalman.
• The 800-ton crane operator failed to identify the obstruction on the slewing path (the 280-ton crane boom
positioned over the pipe rack).
• Failure to develop and implement a formal process or procedure to manage simultaneous crane operations.
• Lack of communication - the 280-ton crane was mobilised with its luffing boom extended approximately 6
metres over the pipe rack into the 800-ton crane’s work area, without coordination.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Always maintain proper coordination with nearby lifting groups when operating cranes near other activities.
• Never slew or reposition a crane without a Signalman’s assistance.
• Implement a formal Simultaneous Operations (SIMOPS) procedure to safely manage multi-crane operations.
• Conduct a pre-lift LMRA to identify potential obstructions in the crane's path.
• Ensure clear and effective communication between crane operators, rigging crews, and other involved teams.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Protective Methods: Failure to warn of hazard

While a Wellhead Engineer was installing a side outlet valve at the wellhead deck, a Floor Man was preparing
downhole guides on the upper deck level, but one down hole guide clamp, weighing 7 kg, slipped and dropped
through open hatch and hit the right middle side of the hard hat above the brim and landed in the grating, causing

WHAT WENT WRONG:
• Inadequate identification of job hazard: The hazards of open hatch, simultaneous operation, drop hazards and its
control measures are not captured in the Job Safety Analysis.
• Inadequate communication between work groups: Toolbox meeting was not conducted between the service
company and the Drilling rig crew who are working in the same area.
• Improper handling of materials: The guide and clamps stored close to the open hatch, not considering or
protecting against the danger of falling objects.
• Inadequate enforcement of PTW: Permit to work was not approved before the start of the work, revalidation of
permit was not followed when job performer changed.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Review Job Safety Analysis / Risk assessment to include all steps, hazards and controls, with focus on the
hazards of simultaneous works, drop objects and line of fire and revise accordingly.
• Ensure proper communication is carried out between work groups and with each work team by coordinating
with different disciplines prior to start.
• Supervisors to ensure that openings are protected with barricades and toe boards to prevent falling objects.
Also, to conduct walk around to identify loose objects and avoid work near openings.
• Ensure that rig crew are conducting campaigns on “Working at heights & dropped objects” elaborating on risk
assessment and situational awareness by carrying out weekly site inspections/ verification.
• Conduct Ad-hoc PTW inspection/ verification walk through spotlighting PTW compliance and hazards of
simultaneous works.

WHAT WENT WRONG:

• The issuing authority must conduct a detailed site inspection before approving a Permit to Work.

detection prior to excavation.

MIDDLE EAST OFFSHORE
DATE: 14 Apr 2025
COUNTRY: Qatar
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Dropped objects
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Safe mechanical lifting
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
After completing the second gyro survey, the crew began rigging down. On the platform deck, a tugger line was
attached to the gyro tool as secondary retention. The tool was lifted to the rig floor using the wireline. Once above
the rotary table, the wireline gooseneck was installed on top of the tool. As the tugger was spooled in to take the
tool’s weight, its swivel caught the gooseneck, pulling it off. The gooseneck, weighing 2.3 kg, fell approximately 50 ft
from the rotary table to the platform deck.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• The securing bolt on the gooseneck was damaged during a previous run and replaced. However, the
replacement bolt lacked the attachment for the secondary gooseneck retention device. As a result, the operation
was carried out without the required safety retention device installed.
• The change of equipment was not escalated and no MOC process was initiated.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Any equipment damage, substitution, or deviation from approved design shall trigger immediate STOP WORK
and be subject to a formal Management of Change process prior to resuming operations.
• Secondary retention devices are safety-critical controls and shall not be removed, bypassed, or omitted without
formal engineering justification and authorization.
• Critical procedural requirements must be complied with at all times, without exception, including during routine,
non-routine, and close-out activities.
• Always follow red zone management, no simultaneous activities during rig-down.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)

NARRATIVE:
The rig crew were in the process of nipple down the bell nipple mandrel. While positioning the multi purpose crane
for installing the bell nipple lifting slings the man basket (354kg), which was holding 2 persons, dislodged from the
main structure of the crane and fell approx.16.5m to the top deck of the platform. Neither of the 2 persons fell as
they were suspended by their harness and inertia reels. Both personnel were recovered in 2 minutes. One of the 2
personnel received first aid treatment for slight swelling.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
1. Rotation of man basket around crane winch drum collar created momentum:
a) System has always been "sticky" with the man basket not self-levelling.
b) Rig crew have developed processes to correct (jumping and operate the winch slightly) that are not included in
the procedures.
2. Crane wire fitted with shackle caught on man basket structure resulted in lift forces.
3. Combination of forces resulted in man basket lifting and twisting away from the sheave.
4. Multipurpose Crane not being operated as per OEM requirements when DMB installed:
a) Man-basket should not move independently of the crane sheave.
b) Moving the controls to the man basket is a requirement within the manual. This releases the drive motor from
the sheave and allows the sheave to rotate freely.
5. Man-basket safety device deployed but not effective:
a) Deemed ineffective following a past incident at another location.
b) OEM’s recommendations regarding the new design and the additional inspections were not considered.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Reinforce the importance of using independent fall arrest equipment when working at height
2. Reinforce the requirement carefully considering attachment points for fall arrest equipment.
3. Ensure that fall arrest equipment is inspected and certified as per Company Procedure.
4. Reinforce the importance of maintaining, storing and inspecting all safety critical equipment to ensure it is in
excellent working order when being used.

PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire

NARRATIVE:
During the workboat transfer operation, workboat was transferred from the laydown area to the transport vessel
main deck and positioned in its transport cradle. During final positioning, the vessel could not remain steady. As a
result, the workboat swung into a nearby Cargo Carrying Unit (CCU), causing damage to the hull. A crew member
handling a tag line was exposed to risk and was nearly caught between the CCU and the swinging workboat.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• Clear Deck policy (no persons on deck during lifting operations) not adhered.
• Use of tag lines should have been properly assessed and if required, deviated against.
• Permit to work not used as per vessel Bridging document, for control of non routine tasks within safety zone.
• Methodology for transferring the workboat was not adequality assessed (MoC) rather a generic lifting risk
assessment was used.
• Banksman did not have direct communication with vessel bridge, who were responsible for vessel positioning.
• Escape route for those involved in lifting route not clear, potential crushing scenario against container on deck,
as work boat swung once lifted out of cradle.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Provide an approved and certified cradle for workboats intended for lifting operations.
• Issue and reinforce a mandatory safety communication during safety meetings emphasizing the requirement for
personnel involved in lifting operations to maintain a clear and unobstructed escape route.
• Review the competency levels of personnel involved in lifting operations and provide retraining where gaps are
identified.
• Issue a formal communication requiring permit-to-work compliance and task-specific risk assessments for all
non-routine activities within designated safety zones.
• Amend the company standard to formally include the prohibition of tag lines and the requirement to maintain a
clear deck policy during boat lifting operations.

NORTH AMERICA ONSHORE
DATE: 20 May 2025
COUNTRY: Canada
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Explosion, fire or burns
ACTIVITY: Maintenance, inspection, testing
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Energy isolation
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
On May 20, 2025, a worker was engaged in repositioning a spec blind from the closed to the open position on the
flare line, in preparation to de-isolate the unit for commissioning activities. During this activity, the worker was
exposed to a gas/energy release from the down steam side of the isolated gate valve at the open flange pair. Worker
required rescue from heights and was provided onsite first aid; worker was transported to a local hospital for
further medical assessment where it was determined worker sustained bruised ribs and a concussion. Worker was
released from hospital the same day.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The 10” gate valve used as a single isolation was not fully closed because the chain operator seized due to physical
interference, giving a false indication that the valve was seated. Pressure verification showed 0 kPag, but this was
ambiguous because the flare system was under slight vacuum, meaning zero pressure did not confirm positive
isolation. Oxygen entered the flare piping system through the partially open valve while the flare remained lit,
creating conditions for ignition. When work was performed on the spectacle blind, this led to a deflagration and an
uncontrolled release of energy that injured the worker.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Zero pressure does not equal positive isolation - Pressure indication alone is an insufficient barrier for verifying
isolation in flare systems, especially where vacuum conditions can exist.
2. Single isolation is not a robust barrier for breaking containment - Single isolation provides little tolerance for
hidden failures and should not be relied upon where severe energy release is credible.
3. Equipment condition and work environment directly shape human decision-making - People act on the cues the
system gives them; degraded equipment and obstructed layouts can actively mislead competent workers.
4. Permits and risk classification must reflect real hazard potential - Administrative controls lose credibility when
they do not reflect the true severity of the hazard.

NARRATIVE:
During a fluid-hauling task, water transfer to a tank truck was completed and the hose was disconnected. A valve
was found not fully closed, and hot fluid sprayed during subsequent valve manipulation. The job was stopped,
emergency medical response was initiated, and the well/site was shut down to support response and control the
release.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Residual energy remained in the system at the time of disconnection/valve manipulation, resulting in a hot-fluid spray.
The investigation identified gaps in procedural requirements for verifying zero energy and specifying chemical PPE for
hot-fluid tasks, and noted that the system configuration did not readily allow field verification of “zero energy.”
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
Update procedures and minimum PPE requirements for hot-fluid tasks (including defined thresholds) and
incorporate explicit “verify zero energy” expectations. Where verification is not practicable, implement engineering/
administrative improvements (e.g., bleed/verification points or safer valve/coupler configurations) so that residual
energy can be confirmed and controlled before disconnecting equipment.

NARRATIVE:
A Mechanic and an E-Tech were repairing a section of the natural gas manifold on frac pump. The employees were
replacing a section on the manifold referred to as a pistol. After the repairs were made the employees opened
the natural gas supply valve to supply the gas manifold on the pump. The mechanic stepped up onto a platform to

the mechanic (IP) opened the main ball valve, both employees heard a loud pop noise. The top of the low-pressure

laceration. The top of the VDR is made of aluminum and weighs approximately 1lb/~454g. The IP was evaluated at a
local emergency room, and the IP received 8 sutures to close the laceration.
WHAT WENT WRONG:

• Worker was new to position (little over 3 months) and never worked on gas train.

place.

testing regulators before leaving the test stand and putting the pump into service.

running gas including all hookup and parts that are approved.

NORTH AMERICA OFFSHORE
DATE: 14 Oct 2025
COUNTRY: USA
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Falls from height
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Working at height
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
A worker fell approximately 16 feet from an aerial work platform onto a Christmas tree cart. The incident occurred
while the worker was using a rope tied to the basket to pull an umbilical and create slack for a storm loop. The rope
failed under tension, releasing stored energy that transferred to the basket. This sudden release caused the basket
to jolt, ejecting the worker.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The task was executed outside equipment design intent, with a man-riding work basket simultaneously used to
pull a load, creating uncontrolled stored energy and disabling effective engineered safeguards. The activity was
not recognised or managed as a lifting operation, resulting in inadequate planning, inappropriate equipment
selection, and exposure of a person to the line of fire when the rope failed. These failures were reinforced by unclear
procedures, fragmented task briefings, and ineffective supervision, allowing unsafe deviations to become normalised.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Inspection and maintenance for man-riding and lifting equipment must meet or exceed manufacturer
requirements, particularly under heavy or harsh operating conditions. Inspection scope, frequency, and competency
should scale with equipment usage and environmental exposure—not minimum internal checklists.
2. Checklist effectiveness depends as much on quality, compliance, and competency as the checklist itself. Poor
design, superficial completion, or unclear roles can create false assurance and allow serious hazards to persist.
3. Safe operation of critical equipment requires clear, shared accountability across suppliers, contractors, and asset
owners. Pre-mobilization checks, acceptance inspections, condition monitoring, and post-event inspections must
be treated as mandatory control points throughout the equipment lifecycle—not administrative steps.

NARRATIVE:
Following heavy rainfall, landslide occurred in the area behind the ten wagon-type cabins (accommodation, canteen,
washing, changing, and rest facilities) located at the oil well site. A ground instability and multiple surface cracks
were identified in the surrounding area.
Personnel were immediately informed of the hazardous ground conditions and instructed to remain vigilant and
exercise caution.
As a preventive control measure, the wagon-type units were relocated to a safer area to eliminate the risk of impact
from further ground movement.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• Inadequate assessment of ground stability.
• Insufficient drainage and erosion control measures.
• Lack of preventive geotechnical monitoring.
• Temporary facilities positioned in potentially hazardous zone.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• A geotechnical assessment should be conducted before positioning cabins, especially in areas prone to heavy
rainfall, slopes, or loose soil conditions.
• Effective surface water drainage and erosion control measures must be implemented to prevent water
accumulation and soil weakening.
• Surface cracks and minor soil movement must be treated as serious warning indicators. A formal inspection
and reporting system should be established for ground condition monitoring.
• Heavy rainfall scenarios should be included in site risk assessments, particularly for temporary infrastructure.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)

NARRATIVE:
A dropped object incident occurred while lowering an overdrive with the casing joint held stationary in the elevator.
The mud saver (component of overdrive) contacted top of the liner joint in the rotary, causing failure at the
connection to the mandrel. The mud saver (~40 kg) fell ~14 meters to the rig floor.
Two personnel were in the red zone at the time (required for the task).
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Overdrive mud saver (~40kg) contacted the top of a liner joint causing a weak point failure and fell ~14m to the rig
floor.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
Learning 1. Procedures for Operating Drilling Equipment:
a. Do our procedures clearly specify the use of proper speed limits during high-risk operations like casing/liner
running operations?
Learning 2. Red Zone Management Opportunities:
a. Does your Red Zone Management Procedure include a clear task level activity matrix or equivalent and include
standardized two-way communication protocols for entry and exit?
b. Was an Early Design Red Zone risk assessment conducted to identify equipment selection and installation
opportunities that reduce Red Zone risk profile?
Learning 3. Automation and Equipment Integration for managing the Red Zone:
a. In Early Design Red Zone risk assessment, have you tried automation tools or equipment upgrades to make
operations safer and reduce Red Zone exposure?
b. Can Red Zone monitoring systems be integrated with the equipment control system to alert the operator when
personnel are in a Red Zone when equipment is moving?

PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Bypassing safety controls
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Work authorization
NARRATIVE:
During the installation of a subsea telescopic clamp on the well shaft beneath the offshore platform, the Diving
Service team encountered a safety-critical situation when a support vessel unexpectedly approached the platform,
despite all established safety measures being in place. The vessel’s captain was promptly contacted and informed
that underwater diving operations were in progress.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• The support vessel entered the platform vicinity without maintaining the required safe distance.
• Insufficient communication with vessel captain.
• While all safety measures on the platform and by the diving team were followed, the control barrier against
external vessel movements failed.
• Reliance on reactive communication (contacting the captain after the approach) rather than proactive control
allowed a near-miss.
• The incident primarily resulted from lack of effective marine coordination and vessel traffic control, leading to a
near-miss with potentially severe consequences for diving operations.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Ensure all vessels operating near offshore platforms are aware of ongoing diving operations.
• Strengthen coordination with support vessels and vessel traffic control to enforce exclusion zones proactively.
• Establish mandatory pre-approach notifications for all vessels near the platform.
• Ensure immediate and continuous communication channels between the platform, diving team, and vessel
captains.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Protective Methods: Failure to warn of hazard

NARRATIVE:
During the inspection of the 8-inch subsea oil and gas pipeline located between offshore platforms, diving
operations were in progress and a scheduled descent from the diving vessel had commenced.
Approximately 15 minutes after the diver entered the water, the vessel’s mechanic reported hull damage resulting in
water ingress into the engine room.
The diver was immediately recovered from the water, and the vessel proceeded toward the platform, where it was
safely moored at the docking bridge.
Following the safe disembarkation of personnel, the damaged vessel was towed to the onshore port by an assisting
tugboat.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• Failure of Vessel Structural Integrity
• Inadequate Pre-Operation Marine Assurance and possible gaps in seaworthiness verification of the vessel
• Inadequate preventive maintenance controls
• Inadequate hull condition monitoring
• Inadequate pre-mobilization inspection and certification checks.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Pre-operation marine inspections must be robust
• Pre-mobilization and daily checks should include:
• Hull condition verification
• Corrosion and structural damage inspection
• Confirmation of valid marine certification
• Review of maintenance status
• Inspection processes must be documented and traceable.

NARRATIVE:
During the heating of an 18-inch pipe to remove the coating, the worker placed the torch at the entrance of the 18-
inch pipe. When attempting to light the torch with a manual spark igniter, a flammable atmosphere was created,
causing a flash fire that resulted in first and second-degree burns to the worker's face after being hit sideways by a
flash fire in the manufacturing workshop area.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• The torch was not in optimal condition (the built-in/manual spark igniter did not work properly).
• Low perception of risk when lighting a torch in a closed environment.
• Incorrect Work Permit (PTW), classified the activity as “cold work” when in fact it involved “high-energy hot
work” with the generation of ignition sources.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Emphasize the responsibilities of workers with roles in the PTW system in the event of serious or fatal workplace
accidents involving their own workers or contractors.
• Conduct an awareness campaign (including contractors) on inspection, reporting, and replacement of tools and
equipment in poor condition (homemade or artisanal tools) before the end of the year.

PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Line of fire

NARRATIVE:
During production tubing running operations on the drilling rig, four metallic components fell from height while
using the catline system.
• Objects dropped from approximately 40 m height
• 2 × 1.8 kg (≈ 706 J each)
• 2 × 10.4 kg (≈ 4,076 J each)
The falling energy was sufficient to cause a fatality.
No injuries occurred, but this qualifies as a High Potential Event (HIPO) due to the severe dropped-object energy.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• Catline anchoring point and installation were modified from the original design without engineering review.
• Assembly was improperly installed and inadequately supported (misaligned rods/spacers, gaps in fittings).
• Refurbished and reused components were not integrity tested; the installed system was not certified to required
load capacity.
• No Management of Change (MOC), risk assessment, or formal operator approval for the modification.
• PTW/JSA did not address the installation change or dropped-object risk.
• Poor communication and oversight between operator and contractor; no operator supervision of the work.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Treat any change to lifting/hoisting equipment or anchoring as a design change requiring MOC, risk assessment,
and operator approval.
• Certification must cover the complete installed system, not only individual components, and must meet
operational load requirements.
• Verify integrity of reused or refurbished parts before use.
• Ensure PTW/JSA reflects actual installation and hazards.
• Clearly define contractor–operator responsibilities and provide supervision for safety-critical work.
• Conduct formal dropped-object inspections after maintenance or modification to derrick equipment.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Protective Methods: Equipment or materials not secured

DATE: 17 Nov 2025
COUNTRY: Brazil
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Explosion, fire or burns
ACTIVITY: Office, warehouse, accommodation, catering
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Work authorization
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Hot work
NARRATIVE:
On 17 November at approximately 09:40, the smoke detector in the laundry room activated after several cleaning
cloths spontaneously combusted shortly after being removed from a dryer and placed on the floor.
The fire brigade responded immediately and extinguished the fire using CO₂ and dry powder extinguishers.
No injuries or asset damage occurred, but the event had potential for a serious fire and smoke exposure.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• Cleaning cloths were likely contaminated with a chemical/oily substance capable of self-heating after drying.
• The chemical hazard was not identified prior to washing and drying.
• Hot cloths were stacked/placed on the floor immediately after drying, allowing heat build-up and ignition.
• No procedure or segregation process existed for handling contaminated rags.
• Personnel did not recognise the chemical odour as a hazard indicator.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Treat cleaning rags as potentially oil/chemical contaminated materials.
• Implement segregation and identification of contaminated cloths before laundering.

DATE: 27 Dec 2025
COUNTRY: Brazil
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Explosion, fire or burns
ACTIVITY: Office, warehouse, accommodation, catering
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Work authorization
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE: Hot work
NARRATIVE:
On 27 December at approximately 07:30, cleaning cloths contaminated with cooking oil were washed and dried in
the laundry.
After drying, the cloths were placed on the floor inside an open bag next to other cloths. Later, all laundry
ventilation, exhaust, and air-conditioning systems were switched off while the room was unattended.
At approximately 13:15, the cloths began releasing smoke and an incipient fire developed. The steward used a dry
chemical extinguisher and the fire brigade extinguished the fire.
No injuries or damage occurred, but the event had serious fire potential.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• Oil-contaminated cloths were washed and dried without special handling precautions.
• Hot cloths were stored in a pile/bag, allowing heat accumulation and self-heating.
• Laundry ventilation and cooling were shut down while the cloths were unattended.
• No procedure existed for segregation, cooling, or disposal of oily rags.
• Hazard of spontaneous combustion from oil-soaked rags was not recognised.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Segregate oil/grease contaminated cloths before laundering.
• Do not place recently dried cloths in piles, bags, or enclosed areas - allow them to cool individually in a
ventilated metal container or spread out.
• Maintain ventilation/exhaust until materials have cooled.
• Implement procedures for handling and disposal of contaminated rags.
• Train personnel on spontaneous combustion risks (oils, hydrocarbons, solvents).
• Provide fire-resistant rag bins and designated storage areas.
